positions.as_written: Measure the sulcus angle on an axial view in flexion, and read the proximal trochlea on a true lateral.
Examine patellar stability between 0 and 30 degrees, because the anatomy makes that the range where soft tissue carries the restraint.
Expect the proximal lateral facet to be the cartilage that fails first, since it takes the highest early pressure.
Leave dysplasia and its grading to 5.12.1 and Section 6.
Treat bony and soft tissue restraint as a handover rather than a sum.
Assess the proximal trochlea specifically on a true lateral radiograph when instability is being investigated, because that is where the geometry varies.
Consider which part of the range a patient's instability occurs in, since the anatomy assigns early flexion to soft tissue and later flexion to bone.
Plan any trochlear work against the notch behind it and the cartilage margins beside it, and 7.56 carries the technique.
Avoid attributing instability to the groove without evidence from the range it controls.
